t: Find Maximum Number of String Pairs
o: All words have length 2 and are distinct; pair i<j when words[i] equals reversed words[j], each word used once, maximize pairs. With n ≤ 50 even checking all O(n²) pairs works, but a hash set of already-seen words answers in one pass: when visiting w, if its reverse was seen before, they form a pair.
k: Words are distinct, so each word has at most one possible partner.
A single pass with a set of seen words counts every pair exactly once (check the reverse before inserting).

a.i: Try every pair i<j and count matches with the reversed string. Simple and sufficient for n ≤ 50.
s: Double loop over all index pairs.
Increment the counter when words[i] == reversed(words[j]).
a.t: O(n² · L) — all pairs with L = 2 comparison cost

a.i: Keep a set of words seen so far. For each new word, if its reverse is already in the set, that reverse can only pair with the current word (distinctness), so count it; otherwise insert the word.
s: Initialize an empty set and counter.
For each word: if reversed(word) is in the set, increment counter; else add word to the set.
a.t: O(n · L) — one pass with O(1) average set operations

w: Mention brute force first, then offer the hash-set pass as the clean optimal. Pitfall: palindromic words like "zz" can never pair with anything (they would need a duplicate, but words are distinct). Follow-up: what if words had varying lengths or duplicates appeared?
